segments.text: In nineteen oh eight, a brewer at Guinness had a problem: he could only test a few batches at a time.
segments.caption: In 1908, a brewer at Guinness had a problem: he could only test a few batches at a time.

segments.text: With so little data, the normal curve made him too confident.
segments.caption: With so little data, the normal curve made him too confident.

segments.text: His fix is the t-distribution.
segments.caption: His fix is the t-distribution.

segments.text: Here's the definition, in simple words.
segments.caption: Here's the definition, in simple words.

segments.text: The t-distribution looks like the normal bell curve, but with fatter tails.
segments.caption: The t-distribution looks like the normal bell curve, but with fatter tails.

segments.text: We use it when the sample is small, and we have to guess the spread from the data itself.
segments.caption: We use it when the sample is small, and we have to guess the spread from the data itself.

segments.text: The smaller the sample, the fatter the tails.
segments.caption: The smaller the sample, the fatter the tails.

segments.text: Why fatter tails? Because with only a few values, our guess of the spread is shaky.
segments.caption: Why fatter tails? Because with only a few values, our guess of the spread is shaky.

segments.text: Take five values, and the spread can look small one time, and big the next.
segments.caption: Take five values, and the spread can look small one time, and big the next.

segments.text: Fatter tails leave room for that extra uncertainty.
segments.caption: Fatter tails leave room for that extra uncertainty.

segments.text: Its exact shape depends on one number: the degrees of freedom.
segments.caption: Its exact shape depends on one number: the degrees of freedom.

segments.text: Usually, that's the sample size, minus one. So five values give four degrees of freedom.
segments.caption: Usually, that's the sample size, minus one. So five values give four degrees of freedom.

segments.text: With four degrees of freedom, the tails are fat.
segments.caption: With four degrees of freedom, the tails are fat.

segments.text: With ten, they slim down.
segments.caption: With ten, they slim down.

segments.text: And by about thirty, the t-curve is almost exactly the normal curve.
segments.caption: And by about thirty, the t-curve is almost exactly the normal curve.

segments.text: Why does this matter? Think about the middle ninety-five percent.
segments.caption: Why does this matter? Think about the middle 95%.

segments.text: On the normal curve, it stretches about two steps from the centre.
segments.caption: On the normal curve, it stretches about two steps from the centre.

segments.text: But with only five values, the t-curve needs about two point eight steps.
segments.caption: But with only five values, the t-curve needs about 2.8 steps.

segments.text: So small samples give wider, more honest ranges.
segments.caption: So small samples give wider, more honest ranges.

segments.text: So remember: the t-distribution is a bell with fatter tails, for small samples.
segments.caption: So remember: the t-distribution is a bell with fatter tails, for small samples.

segments.text: The bigger the sample, the closer it gets to normal.
segments.caption: The bigger the sample, the closer it gets to normal.

segments.text: As the sample grows, what does the t-distribution turn into?

segments.text: The normal distribution!
segments.caption: The normal distribution!

segments.text: With more data, the extra uncertainty fades, and the tails slim down to the normal curve.
